question: Which statement best describes State pseudo-classes: :hover, :focus, :active?
options: These react to user interaction. :hover applies when the pointer is over an element, :focus when it receives keyboard/tab focus (critical for accessibility), and :active during the press. Always pair :hover with :focus so keyboard users get the same feedback, and consider :focus-visible to show outlines only for keyboard navigation.

These match elements by their position among siblings. :first-child / :last-child target the ends; :nth-child(n) takes a formula like 2n (even), odd, or 3n+1. They count ALL siblings, so :nth-child(2) means 'this element AND it is the 2nd child'. Use :nth-of-type when you only want to count elements of the same tag.

Form pseudo-classes reflect input state. :checked targets checked checkboxes/radios and is the key to checkbox-only toggles (the 'CSS checkbox hack'). :disabled, :required, :valid, and :invalid let you style forms purely from their state without JavaScript.

:not(selector) matches every element that does NOT match the inner selector — great for 'all but the last' spacing or excluding a variant. It takes the specificity of its most specific argument (the :not() itself adds none). Modern :not() accepts a comma list: :not(.a, .b).
